idiom_name: one directory/package per domain area, with an explicit published surface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: make each module one unit of the host's grouping mechanism (directory and package, namespace, module file or compilation unit), give it a domain name, and publish a small explicit interface. Derive the partition from the model - concepts that are understood and changed together live together, dependencies run one way and stay acyclic. Inside the module everything that is not part of the published interface stays private by whatever mechanism the language offers; outside, clients see only the published names. Revisit the partition whenever the model deepens: packaging follows understanding, not the other way round. Apply the Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP): no cycles in the module-dependency graph; resolve by merging, extracting an interface, or inverting via events. Follow the Stable Dependencies Principle (SDP): modules that change frequently should not depend on stable ones - unstable policy modules depend on stable mechanism. Follow the Stable Abstractions Principle (SAP): stable modules tend to be more abstract (interfaces, abstract classes), while unstable modules tend to be concrete. A package's abstractness should be proportional to its stability.
code_sketch:
module billing          # one domain area, one name
    invoice, payment, refund      # published concepts
    _ledger, _rate_table          # internal details

module shipping
    shipment, carrier, quote

# clients import only published names; dependencies:
# shipping -> billing  (never billing -> shipping)
pitfalls: Grouping by technical layer instead of by domain concept recreates the scattering the pattern removes.
A catch-all 'common' or 'shared' unit that everything depends on becomes a second global namespace.
Enforcing the boundary only in documentation while the dependency graph stays cyclic.
Feature envy across modules: a class in module A depends heavily on internals of module B without a domain relationship - usually signals the concept lives in the wrong module.
Internal detail leakage: a module's public barrel file re-exports implementation details, hiding which concepts actually belong together and widening the coupling surface.

The 'utils' or 'helpers' anti-pattern: a domain-agnostic catch-all module accumulates unrelated helpers, becoming an untestable dependency magnet that cannot be changed without unpredictable blast radius. Refactor by moving each function to the domain concept it serves.
Entity-based granularity: giving each class its own package creates a dependency explosion where every use case spans many packages; group by aggregate root instead.
The distributed monolith: splitting code into modules but sharing a single database schema means schema changes ripple across module teams; each module should own its schema or database.
Over-refined internal structure: a deeply nested internal/ hierarchy per module makes navigation harder than the original flat structure; prefer a shallow, consistent internal layout.

Cyclic integration events: domain events are the right cross-module channel, but a closed loop of event->handler->event->handler that never terminates indicates the module boundary has been crossed incorrectly; trace the event chain to find where the seam belongs.

Wrong move: treat a directory or project split as the module boundary -> physical separation can still leave shared concepts, rules, and ownership coupled across modules -> instead assign each concept's invariants and behavior to one module and expose only its published interface or events.
sources: Martin Fowler, 'Package Principles' blog series (damonkelley.me, randycoulman.com, 2014) - covers Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP), Stable Dependencies Principle (SDP), and Stable Abstractions Principle (SAP) for package-level design.

Kirk Knoernschild, Java Application Architecture: Modularity Patterns with Examples Using OSGi, Pearson (2012) - 18 modularity patterns including Cohesive Modules, Acyclic Relationships, Published Interface, Module Facade, and Utility Patterns such as Colocate Exceptions.

Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design, Addison-Wesley (2013), Chapter 9 'Modules' - covers module naming conventions, module placement within and across bounded contexts, and the relationship between modules and the ubiquitous language.

Fabian Beck and Stephan Diehl, 'On the Congruence of Modularity and Code Coupling' (FSE 2011) - 16 open-source systems studied showing structural dependencies and evolutionary coupling most strongly congruent with package modularization; none of the modularity principles studied dominates alone.

David B. Binkley et al., 'An Empirical Study of Slice-Based Cohesion and Coupling' (TOSEM 2007) - 22,651 procedures from 63 programs showing slice-based cohesion metrics quantify code quality and track design deterioration over time; baseline cohesion values established for reengineering targets.

Manoel Medeiros, 'Acyclic Dependencies Principle: from monolith to microservice, from graph theory to the cost of change' (2026) - ADP-SDP-SAP trio applied across bounded contexts, microservices, monorepos and polyrepos; event-driven acyclicity and inversion techniques for cycle breaking.
